title: Managing Water Quality in Premise Plumbing (Singh et al., 2020, Water)
text:
Water Article
Managing Water Quality in Premise Plumbing: Subject Matter Experts' Perspectives and a Systematic Review of Guidance Documents
Rajveer Singh, Kerry A. Hamilton, Md Rasheduzzaman, Zhao Yang, Saurajyoti Kar, Angelita Fasnacht, Sheldon V. Masters, Patrick L. Gurian
Department of Civil, Architectural and Environmental Engineering, Drexel University, Philadelphia, PA
Water 2020, 12, 347; doi:10.3390/w12020347

title: Managing Water Quality in Premise Plumbing (Singh et al., 2020, Water)
text: Abstract: Although many guidance documents have been developed to inform the design and operation of building water systems to ensure safe water quality, there is a lack of consensus on some topics. This study interviewed 22 subject matter experts (SMEs) to identify topics of concern for managing water quality in buildings and compared SME views with information available on these topics in 15 systematically screened important guidance documents. The study found 18 design and 11 operational topics as critical for managing water quality in buildings. No one guidance document addressed all these topics, suggesting that a compendium of available guidance is needed. SMEs most frequently recommended temperature and residual disinfectant measurements as good parameters for monitoring overall building water quality. Both SME and guidance document recommendations for temperature for controlling opportunistic pathogen growth were reasonably consistent with water heater setpoint >60C. However, hot water temperature recommendations varied between 50 and 55C for other locations (i.e., the water temperature at the tap or end of the return loop). On the contrary, recommendations for disinfectant residual levels (0.2-2.0 mg/L), flushing frequency (1-14 days), and allowable time for hot water to reach the tap (10-60 s) were not consistent. While this study was able to reconcile diverging views on some of the water quality topics, such as identifying common guidance for water heater set point to at least 60C, it also highlights lack of definitive guidance on other critical topics, such as residual level, flushing frequency, hot water time to tap, and the use of thermostatic mixing valves, indicating that these are significant knowledge gaps that need further investigation. The study concludes that there is a need for developing evidence-based guidance, particularly on the topics where expert opinions diverged.

title: Managing Water Quality in Premise Plumbing (Singh et al., 2020, Water)
text: Keywords: Legionella; opportunistic premise plumbing pathogens; water quality in buildings; guidance documents; water heater setpoint temperature; disinfectant residual; mycobacteria

title: Managing Water Quality in Premise Plumbing (Singh et al., 2020, Water)
text:
1. Introduction
Water quality in the water supplier's distribution system is subject to monitoring and regulation, but once water enters a building plumbing system, the responsibility for maintaining water quality shifts to the building owner, occupants, and/or facility manager. In many cases, these stakeholders are not water quality specialists but nevertheless must address an array of water quality concerns. These concerns are driven by the potential for water quality to deteriorate in building plumbing systems due to chemical and biological reactions in the bulk water and interactions with pipe surfaces. One manner in which water quality may deteriorate in buildings is through the growth of opportunistic premise plumbing pathogens (OPPPs) (i.e., Legionella pneumophila, non-tuberculous mycobacteria, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, etc.), which can be enabled by the loss of residual disinfectant over extended residence times. Extended residence times in building plumbing can also allow for corrosion (which may release copper and lead) and the continued formation of disinfection byproducts (DBPs) (TTHMs, HAAs).

title: Managing Water Quality in Premise Plumbing (Singh et al., 2020, Water)
text: Management guidance has focused primarily on preventing Legionnaires' disease, as this is a US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reportable illness (the only one caused by opportunistic pathogens known to be found in building plumbing), has been associated with high litigation costs, and has driven public concerns. To address these risks, numerous federal, state, and local agencies and organizations worldwide have developed guidance for managing water quality in buildings, many of which focus on Legionella control.

title: Managing Water Quality in Premise Plumbing (Singh et al., 2020, Water)
text:
Despite the existence of guidance documents, this guidance is not always consistent across sources. Guidance documents do not always explain the underlying causal model and full evidence basis for their recommendations, which makes it difficult to understand why recommendations may differ or where the evidence base is lacking. In addition, guidance documents are, by their nature, consensus documents and may have gaps where consensus cannot be reached. In contrast, subject matter experts (SMEs) can provide perspectives on causal models and the strength of available evidence that may be missing or implicit in guidance documents and can provide views on areas for which consensus has not yet been reached. 2. Data Sources and Methodologies
This study identified critical issues for maintaining water quality in building plumbing systems through semi-structured interviews of SMEs and contrasted this information with that obtained from a review of existing guidance documents on water quality in building plumbing systems.

title: Managing Water Quality in Premise Plumbing (Singh et al., 2020, Water)
text:
Subject Matter Experts Consultations
A snowball sampling approach was used for recruiting subject matter experts (SMEs) with interdisciplinary backgrounds from across the United States. Among 36 SMEs contacted, 22 agreed to participate, including experts from academic research (41%), government (27%), the plumbing or facilities management industry (18%), and drinking water utilities (14%). SMEs participated in a roughly 1 h semi-structured phone interview discussing operational and design parameters with the most significant impact on water quality, appropriate indicators, existing sources of guidance, monitoring tools, and significant knowledge gaps.

title: Managing Water Quality in Premise Plumbing (Singh et al., 2020, Water)
text:
Existing Guidance and Selection of Important Guidance Documents (IGDs)
A pool of 54 building water quality guidance documents from various federal, state, and local agencies and professional organizations from the United States and worldwide was identified. The guidance documents were separated into two tiers. The first tier, referred to as important guidance documents (IGDs), consisted of 15 documents that were searched for all topics identified by the SME interviews. The remaining 39 documents were consulted only when a topic identified by the SME interviews was not addressed in the IGDs. Guidance documents were selected as IGDs for either of two reasons: (1) the document was specifically identified by multiple SMEs as important and (2) a keyword search indicated that the document covered a high percentage of topics identified as relevant by SMEs.

title: Managing Water Quality in Premise Plumbing (Singh et al., 2020, Water)
text:
Table 2 and Table 3: Design and Operational Factors
Design factors viewed unfavorably by both SMEs and guidance documents (related to increased water age/residence time): distant taps/devices, low flow fixtures, oversized pipe diameters, building size, building layout, poor hydraulics (dead ends, short circuiting, long travel times), green buildings, flexible shower hoses, pipes exposed to temperature extremes, electronic (automatic) faucets. Thermostatic mixing valves (TMVs) received mixed views: favorable for enabling high water temperatures elsewhere in the system while protecting against scalding at the point of use (OSHA 1996; WHO 2007; CDC 2003), but unfavorable because they create a favorable temperature zone for opportunistic pathogen growth across the thermal gradient at the valve, can fail and allow hot/cold mixing, and biofilms on the valve itself can contribute to pathogen growth (NASEM 2019; WHO 2011).

title: Managing Water Quality in Premise Plumbing (Singh et al., 2020, Water)
text: Pipe material views: copper has antimicrobial properties but pathogens like Legionella may develop resistance; PVC and PEX pipe may leach organic carbon that enhances OPPP growth; the UK Department of Health identified British Standard 6920 as applicable to PEX pipe, while NASEM 2019 indicated a need for US standards addressing microbial growth potential of PEX.

title: Managing Water Quality in Premise Plumbing (Singh et al., 2020, Water)
text: Operational factors: Six factors related to water age (low demand/under-occupancy, infrequently used fixtures, high water age, high carbon/nutrient water) were viewed negatively by both SMEs and guidance documents. Maintaining disinfectant residual was viewed favorably by 12 SMEs and 12 guidance documents; loss of residual was viewed unfavorably. Chloramine rather than chlorine was favored by 10 SMEs and 4 guidance documents (more persistent, better able to penetrate biofilms, but risk of nitrification if residual not maintained; less clarity on impact on mycobacteria, which are more resistant to disinfection generally). "Keep hot water hot and cold water cold" was endorsed by 6 SMEs and 12 guidance documents. Water heater temperature control was favorably mentioned by 14 SMEs and 7 guidance documents with zero unfavorable mentions. Flushing received 12 favorable and 3 unfavorable mentions from SMEs, and 10 favorable and 0 unfavorable mentions from guidance documents (favorable: brings fresh residual disinfectant and controls microbial growth; unfavorable: may bring more nutrients/carbon to pipe biofilm and stress biofilms leading to detachment of pathogens into bulk water).

title: Managing Water Quality in Premise Plumbing (Singh et al., 2020, Water)
text: The National Academies report (NASEM 2019) covers the most topics of any single guidance document: 16 of 18 design topics and 10 of 10 operational topics it addresses. The second and third highest coverage were WHO 2007 and CDC 2003.

title: Managing Water Quality in Premise Plumbing (Singh et al., 2020, Water)
text:
Indicators of water quality
SMEs identified eight general indicators of water quality measurable in buildings. Residual disinfectant and temperature were the most commonly mentioned indicators (9 and 7 mentions respectively) and both were generally seen as good indicators (residual: 7 of 9 mentions positive; temperature: 7 of 7 mentions positive). Measures of specific opportunistic pathogens were not widely endorsed as an indicator, largely because of the expense and difficulty of measuring them directly. Time required for hot water temperature to stabilize at the tap ("time to tap") was mentioned by only two SMEs but both saw it as a good indicator supplementing a simple temperature reading, since it also reflects flow balance in the system.

title: Managing Water Quality in Premise Plumbing (Singh et al., 2020, Water)
text:
Table 6: Significant Knowledge Gap Issues (from SME disagreement or consensus)
1. Flushing (Operational): Determine optimum flushing frequency considering the tradeoff between residual replenishment and OPPP nutrient feeding. [Disagreement among SMEs and guidance documents]
2. Residual levels (Operational): Determine optimum numerical values for residual concentrations under different conditions, balancing OPPP control against disinfection byproduct (DBP) formation tradeoffs. [Disagreement among SMEs and guidance documents]
3. Thermostatic mixing valves (Design): Investigate TMVs as problematic elements for OPPP growth and whether alternative designs or proper maintenance can resolve issues. [Disagreement among SMEs]
4. Chloramine vs. chlorine (Operational): Investigate tradeoffs between disinfectants and whether chloramines are effective for mycobacteria control. [Disagreement among SMEs and guidance documents]
5. Temperature control strategy (Design and operational): Despite consensus on temperature effects on Legionella, there is a lack of consensus on the emphasis on temperature vs. hydraulics vs. mixing valves for OPPP control. Roughly two approaches: (1) use high temperature (60C heater setpoint), or (2) use more moderate temperature (49-55C heater setpoint) but require short flow times and limited temperature drops in pipes. [Disagreement among SMEs]
6. Water heater type (Design): Compare water quality of on-demand tankless heaters with tanked heaters. [Consensus gap among SMEs]
7-8. Pipe materials (Design): Investigate suitable pipe materials or anti-microbial coatings for OPPP growth; investigate copper's impact on Legionella and other OPPPs, leaching properties, and compatibility with hot water. [Consensus gap among SMEs]
9. Control strategy (Operational): Does temperature control work for mycobacteria and other OPPPs too? How do microbial communities adapt/shift with temperature changes? [Consensus gap among SMEs]
10-11. OPPP characterization: Legionella (and other OPPP) growth characterization with respect to temperature, time, residuals, nutrients; standardize OPPP characterization techniques and identify factors associated with OPPP concentration and health risk. [Consensus gap among SMEs]

title: Managing Water Quality in Premise Plumbing (Singh et al., 2020, Water)
text:
Conclusions
This study used SME interviews to identify 18 critical design topics and 11 critical operational topics for ensuring water quality in building plumbing systems. While no one guidance document covers all 29 topics identified by the SMEs, the 2019 National Academies (NASEM) report was the most comprehensive, covering 26 topics (16 design and 10 operational), followed by WHO 2007 and CDC 2003, with 15 and 14 topics covered respectively. Recommendations for water heater setpoint were consistent across the five water quality guidance documents that made specific recommendations, all recommending at least 60C. However, guidance on temperature in the plumbing distribution system was not completely consistent, with recommendations from water quality guidance documents falling in the 50-55C range, while the International Plumbing Code requires <43C (a scald-safety requirement in direct tension with Legionella-control temperature guidance). This study provides a compendium of the divergent views and lack of guidance through a systematic study design and analysis, and recommends developing evidence-based guidance particularly on topics that lack guidance or present split opinions, such as residual level, flushing frequency, hot water time to tap, and the use of thermostatic mixing valves.

title: Practitioners' Perspective on Legionella Control Practices (Singh et al., 2022, Water)
text:
Water Article
Practitioners' Perspective on the Prevalent Water Quality Management Practices for Legionella Control in Large Buildings in the United States
Rajveer Singh, Deepika Chauhan, Alanna Fogarty, Md Rasheduzzaman, Patrick L. Gurian
Water 2022, 14, 663; https://doi.org/10.3390/w14040663

title: Practitioners' Perspective on Legionella Control Practices (Singh et al., 2022, Water)
text: Abstract: Managing building water systems is complicated by the need to maintain hot water temperatures high enough to control the growth of Legionella spp. while minimizing the risk of scalding. This study assessed water quality management practices in large buildings in the United States. Surveys conducted with building water quality managers found that more than 85% of buildings have hot water temperatures that are consistent with scald risk mitigation guidelines (i.e., <122F/50C). However, nearly two thirds and three quarters of buildings do not comply with the common temperature guidance for opportunistic pathogen control, i.e., water heater setpoint >140F (60C) and recirculation loop >122F (50C), respectively; median values for both setpoint and recirculation loop temperatures are 10F (6C) or more below temperatures recommended for opportunistic pathogen control. These observations suggest that many buildings are prone to Legionella spp. risk. The study also found that 27% of buildings do not comply with guidelines for time to equilibrium hot water temperature, over 33% fail to monitor temperature in the recirculation loop, more than 70% fail to replace or disinfect showerheads, more than 40% lack a written management plan, and only a minority conduct any monitoring of residual disinfectant levels or microbiological quality.

title: Practitioners' Perspective on Legionella Control Practices (Singh et al., 2022, Water)
text: Keywords: building water quality management; opportunistic premise plumbing pathogens (OPPPs); Legionella spp.; temperature control; COVID-19; recirculation loop; thermostatic mixing valve (TMV)

title: Practitioners' Perspective on Legionella Control Practices (Singh et al., 2022, Water)
text:
1. Introduction
Building plumbing systems often have conditions conducive to the growth of opportunistic premise plumbing pathogens (OPPPs), particularly Legionella spp. In the United States, Legionnaires' disease cases increased 5.5-fold in recent years, from 0.42 per 100,000 population in 2000 to 2.29 per 100,000 population in 2017, and the number of outbreaks nearly quadrupled from 2009 to 2017. A glaring example of building plumbing system failure is the public health crisis in Flint, Michigan in 2014, where aging plumbing infrastructure contributed to public exposure to elevated lead concentrations, as well as a subsequent outbreak of Legionnaires' disease.

title: Practitioners' Perspective on Legionella Control Practices (Singh et al., 2022, Water)
text: Temperature control in building plumbing is a tradeoff between Legionella spp. growth and scalding risk. While higher temperatures provide safety against Legionella spp. growth but cause risk of scalding, lower temperatures are favorable to Legionella spp. growth but are safe against scalding. There is a tentative consensus on maintaining the water heater setpoint temperature at 140F (60C) for preventing Legionella spp. risk, but there is less agreement on the recommended hot water temperature in the distribution system. The majority of guidance documents recommend keeping hot water, including in recirculation loops and distal taps, at higher than 122-124F (50-51C), with others recommending higher than 131F (55C). Rasheduzzaman et al. (2020), in a meta-analysis of hotel plumbing systems, recommended 59C (138F) as the temperature required to keep the risk of detectable Legionella spp. below 10% (although limited data were consistent with 50C (122F) being sufficient to limit Legionella spp. to levels <1000 CFU/L).

title: Practitioners' Perspective on Legionella Control Practices (Singh et al., 2022, Water)
text: For safety against scalding, temperatures below 122-124F (50-51C) are recommended by one set of guidance documents, while temperatures below 110F (43C) are recommended by another set applicable to buildings with vulnerable populations, such as hospitals and long-term care facilities. Time to tap: a value of 60 s or less at the point of use is generally regarded as an indicator of good plumbing hydraulics (short pipe runs, good flow balance) sufficient for OPPP control; lower values between 10 and 30 s have been recommended in other guidance documents. Thermostatic mixing valves (TMVs) have both favorable and unfavorable aspects and are therefore recommended not to be used in high-risk buildings. Issues with TMVs include leaching from organic, synthetic, or metal-based manufacturing materials, design malfunction, and dead water volume at tepid temperatures. Similar issues are noted for flexible shower hoses and electronic faucets. Other problematic spots include cooling towers, hot tubs (spas), centralized atomizers/misters/humidifiers, decorative fountains, dead ends, and low-flow fixtures.

title: Practitioners' Perspective on Legionella Control Practices (Singh et al., 2022, Water)
text:
2. Methods
Semi-structured interviews and online surveys were conducted with building facility managers to collect information on critical issues of building water quality management. The interview protocol contained questions covering building characteristics, plumbing design, water quality monitoring parameters, problematic features, management programs, and control measures. Temperature monitoring at three critical points-heater setpoint, temperature in recirculation loop, and temperature at the faucet/point of use (POU)-were included, along with time to tap. A total of 15 facility managers participated in semi-structured phone interviews and 34 facility managers responded to an online (Qualtrics) survey; after removing incomplete responses, the combined database included 41 facility managers. Seventeen of 41 participants (42%) were from buildings with high-vulnerability residents (hospitals, retirement homes/long-term care facilities); the rest were classified as low-vulnerability. 93% of buildings had centralized water heating systems and 85% had recirculation systems.

3.3 Temperature Monitoring Results (Table 4) WATER HEATER SETPOINT TEMPERATURE:

RECIRCULATION LOOP TEMPERATURE:
- Guidance for microbial control: >=122F (>=50C) [WHO 2007; European Guidelines Working Group 2017]
- Actual survey results: N=24, median = 110F (43C), range 90-179F (32-82C), std dev 20F (11C)
- Only 25% of buildings were in compliance (27% low-vulnerability, 22% high-vulnerability)

- Guidance: <9F (<5C) [ASPE 2008]
- Actual survey results: N=22, median = 13F (7C), std dev 12F (7C)
- Only 26% of buildings were in compliance (39% low-vulnerability, 15% high-vulnerability) TIME TO TAP:
- Guidance: 122-131F (50-55C) at POU within 60 sec [European Guidelines Working Group 2017]; >=131F (>=55C) at distal point within 60 sec [NASEM 2020]
- Actual survey results: 0-30s (N=18, 49%); 31-60s (N=9, 24%); >60s (N=10, 27%)
- 73% of buildings were in compliance with at least two of three time-to-tap guidance documents; 27% exceeded 60 seconds, failing all three.

title: Practitioners' Perspective on Legionella Control Practices (Singh et al., 2022, Water)
text:
Discussion of temperature-scald tradeoff
A National Academy of Science, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) report on Legionella management in premise plumbing summarizes the comparison of Legionella and scalding risk at different temperatures: 110F (43C) causes nearly no scald risk (several minutes, >35 min, required to cause first-degree burns) but high Legionella growth potential. In contrast, 120F (49C) may cause low-to-moderate scald risk (first- and second-degree burns for exposures >1 min and >5 min respectively) and moderate-to-very-low Legionella risk. The paper argues that 110F (43C) at point of use should be reserved for buildings where occupants cannot remove themselves from scalding water (e.g., very young, elderly, or disabled residents); for buildings where occupants can avoid prolonged exposure, 120F (49C) may be an acceptable point-of-use temperature. Where point-of-use temperature must be kept below 110F (43C) to protect vulnerable occupants, Legionella/OPPP risk should be mitigated through other controls: maintaining minimum disinfectant residual, low residence time (flushing), good hydraulics (low time-to-tap), appropriate plumbing materials, and aerosol control, or combinations of these.

title: Practitioners' Perspective on Legionella Control Practices (Singh et al., 2022, Water)
text:
Problematic Features (Figure 3)
The most frequently reported potentially-problematic features, especially in high-vulnerability buildings (35% or more prevalence): thermostatic mixing valves (TMVs), electronic faucets, flexible shower hoses, and hot/cold water pipes running together (allowing hot water to cool and cold water to warm toward temperatures favorable for OPPP growth). TMVs were more commonly reported at individual fixtures (41% high-vulnerability, 17% low-vulnerability buildings) than as a single centralized TMV after the water heater (6% high-vulnerability, 13% low-vulnerability). Other problematic features: cooling towers and return loops. Frequencies of problematic features were generally higher in high-vulnerability buildings, except cooling towers and seldom-used fixtures, which were more frequent in low-vulnerability buildings.

title: Practitioners' Perspective on Legionella Control Practices (Singh et al., 2022, Water)
text:
4. Discussion
Results indicate hot water temperatures in a large number of building plumbing systems are NOT in compliance with guidance for Legionella control. Both median setpoint (130F/54C) and recirculation loop (110F/43C) temperatures were at least 10F (6C) lower than corresponding recommended minimums (140F/60C and 122F/50C respectively). The above observations indicate that prioritization of scalding risk over Legionella growth risk is common in actual practice. This is confirmed by the high frequency of Legionella detection in building plumbing systems, including hospitals and other high-vulnerability buildings, and increasing Legionnaires' disease cases in the United States.

title: Practitioners' Perspective on Legionella Control Practices (Singh et al., 2022, Water)
text: Regular monitoring is recommended to ensure water quality parameters stay within guidance limits and to catch unanticipated changes, but though direct Legionella monitoring is one of the most essential parts of water quality management practice in Europe, no federal regulations require it in the US and available directives/standards are inconsistent. This study's monitoring data show that while >80% of buildings monitored setpoint and faucet temperatures, significantly lower percentages monitored return loop (<67%) and distal tap (<35%) temperatures - a gap in monitoring precisely the locations most vulnerable to Legionella growth. Disinfectant residual, pH, and hardness were measured in 25% or fewer of buildings, likely reflecting the complexity of the methods/techniques required and/or a lack of training among facility managers.

title: Practitioners' Perspective on Legionella Control Practices (Singh et al., 2022, Water)
text: The problematic features identified (TMVs, electronic faucets, flexible shower hoses) share a common risk driver: potential for materials used in their construction to promote microbial growth, in addition to their tendency to create lukewarm-water zones. The benefits and risks of TMVs remain unclear even in guidance documents and the scientific literature; some high-vulnerability buildings (particularly hospitals) in this study used them extensively while demonstrating negative Legionella monitoring results, indicating that proper materials selection and maintenance can mitigate the TMV risk. Only 59% of high-vulnerability and 29% of low-vulnerability buildings had a written water management plan, despite the CDC toolkit's recommendation that high-risk buildings maintain one. No single guidance document was used predominantly by facility managers - this reinforces that no one guidance document provides all information applicable to complex building plumbing scenarios, and multiple documents typically need to be consulted (e.g., ASHRAE 188 provides a general risk-management framework but not specific numeric guidance; the CDC's toolkit fills in some of the implementation specifics for ASHRAE 188).

title: Practitioners' Perspective on Legionella Control Practices (Singh et al., 2022, Water)
text: For showers - one of the highest-risk fixtures for Legionella due to aerosolization - 65% of high-vulnerability buildings reported self-draining hoses and 29% reported frequent shower head replacement/disinfection; 29% of high-vulnerability buildings had neither control measure in place, and 54% of low-vulnerability buildings had neither.

title: Practitioners' Perspective on Legionella Control Practices (Singh et al., 2022, Water)
text:
5. Conclusions
Current hot water management practices in the US are aligned more with preventing scald risk than controlling OPPPs, which may explain the constantly increasing Legionnaires' disease burden. Nearly two-thirds and three-quarters of surveyed buildings do not comply with common temperature guidance for opportunistic pathogen control at the water heater setpoint (>=140F/60C) and recirculation loop (>=122F/50C) respectively - more than 10F (6C) below recommended values - and temperature loss from heater to tap fails to meet the <9F (<5C) guidance in three-quarters of buildings. A large number of buildings lack critical management strategies: 33% fail to monitor recirculation loop temperature, 70% fail to disinfect or replace shower heads annually, 40% lack a written management plan, and fewer than 10% monitor residual disinfectant levels or microbial water quality. The paper recommends developing formal training guidelines for facility managers and notes the value of a decision support tool that provides on-demand, tailored guidance specific to a building's needs (citing Rasheduzzaman et al. 2021, "Conceptualization to Development of a Decision Support Tool to Manage Building Water Quality" - the PIPE tool's own research lineage).
